postTitle: Leadership reportedly pressured young male staff to try breast milk
postDescription: People around the office were exchanging shocked messages after an HR call this morning. Apparently the CEO repeatedly asked young male employees to try her breast milk and a formal complaint was filed. Colleagues say about 95 percent of the union signed a letter to the board calling out favoritism and lack of accountability, and the board has not replied even after almost three weeks. The employee most affected was offered a new role and is conflicted about leaving a program they built while everything else feels uncertain, and there is even talk of a government shutdown looming. Has anyone seen similar boundary crossing from senior leaders, or tips on safe confidential steps colleagues can take yaar?

replies.text: Exactly. If HR records are sticky, screenshots and personal notes with dates help later. Also check if the union letter mentions any ask for independent investigator.

comments.text: Practical steps: encourage the complainant to get legal advice, ask union to push for an external independent enquiry, and escalate to labour or regulatory body if board ignores it. replies.text: Thanks, will pass this along. People I spoke with are scared to talk openly, and they worry retaliation will be ignored. Any tips on anonymising evidence before giving to union?
Use personal emails, cloud backups not linked to work, and keep a dated log. If possible get witness statements in writing, even short messages help.

comments.text: Board thinks it is dramatic so do nothing. Classic. Imagine treating a formal complaint like a soap opera. 🤦‍♂️

replies.text: Sarcasm aside, that reaction is dangerous. Boards have fiduciary duties, and ignoring harassment risks legal fallout.

comments.text: From a policy angle: insist on an independent investigator, timeline for response, and preserve chain of custody for records. If the board stalls, regulatory complaint and media escalation are options but need careful planning with counsel.

replies.text: Good point about timeline. Colleagues said the union demanded a response but board called the letter dramatic and did nothing. Do we know common timelines for independent probes?

comments.text: Feeling badly for the person who built the program. Tough call to leave something you made. Hope the union offers real support, not just signatures.
Quick skeptical take: make sure details are verified before full escalation, false rumours can ruin careers too. But if complaint filed, treat it seriously and protect people involved.

replies.text: Agree to verify, but the presence of a formal complaint and union letter already gives weight. Precaution and protection should go hand in hand.

postTitle: Is my new hire working a second job during work hours?
postDescription: Heard a voicemail tone from my new hire's phone that sounded like a client booking and it stuck with me. The person never disclosed any other job, but small signs — phone voicemails, slow responses, slipping deadlines — are stacking up and I am worried it is a second gig during breaks. I hired them for full time work and now daily priorities are getting delayed, team is covering extra tasks and trust is getting thoda shaky. I have not raised it yet because I do not want to jump to conclusions or look petty, but performance conversations are looming. Anyone here dealt with this kind of scene — how did you handle proof, HR, and the awkward talk? 😕

comments.text: This happened at my last job yaar. One person was freelancing during lunch and then started missing deliverables. We documented missed SLAs, had a private chat, gave clear expectations and a final warning. If they keep juggling, it becomes performance issue not morality.

replies.text: Agree. Documentation is the only defence if it goes south. Also check company moonlighting policy before accusing.
Thanks, I will start a simple log of missed items today. Do you remember how you framed the one on one? Thoda nervous about sounding accusatory.

comments.text: First, check the employment agreement and any moonlighting clause. Second, talk to them about performance with examples not assumptions. If your org has an HR policy on second jobs you can rely on that for next steps, warna just stick to facts.

replies.text: Yes, policy is key. Also be mindful of local labour law on outside employment, some places allow it unless it affects work.

comments.text: Welcome to the side hustle era where everyone is CEO of their own lunchtime enterprise. If they billed during office hours, that's not hustle, it's time theft. 😤

Don’t start by searching phones or eavesdropping. Set a short performance improvement plan with measurable KPIs, one week checks. If metrics improve, great. If not, you have a fair reason to escalate.

replies.text: Good point, metrics protect both sides. I will pull weekly task reports and share clear expectations in writing, that feels less personal.

comments.text: Maybe there is financial pressure too, we had someone juggling to pay bills. Tried to be empathetic, offered flexible hours but set clear output rules. Sometimes small support fixes the scene, other times it does not.

Log timestamps, missed deadlines, and customer impact. Ask HR about conflict of interest and whether undisclosed external work violates contract. If you confront, keep it about work impact only, not moral judgement.

replies.text: Also check if company has a disclosure process — some firms allow outside work if declared.

postTitle: Team nearby resisting any change after bad leadership

Now Sara is collaborating more, running honest 1on1s and small wins are happening, but old habits are sticking for some and morale swings a lot. replies.text: And you know the fun part, they will still complain about every tiny change for months. Classic human behaviour lol.

replies.text: This. And document those quick wins publicly so people see progress, otherwise old cynicism kicks in.

replies.text: Agree. Also track behavior metrics not just delivery metrics. Culture problems show up in attrition and engagement scores.

postTitle: 85 percent invisibility and my daily masking grind
postDescription: At a team lunch someone quietly told me they never disclose their neurodiversity because they think it will kill their career. The story says 85 to 90 percent of neurodiverse people in India stay underemployed and end up hiding their conditions. I have been masking a lot too in meetings, forcing eye contact, scripting replies, and it drains me, productivity suffers and small mistakes happen. Minor accommodations would fix a lot but the culture still makes disclosure feel like a gamble, only about 3 percent see any real advantage. Kya karna chahiye — how do you decide when to tell, or how to push for small changes without getting boxed in? 😕

comments.text: That hits home yaar. I used to sit next to someone who would fake note taking just to hide they needed quiet time. They eventually left because asking for simple things was seen as weakness.

replies.text: Sorry to hear that, that sounds rough. How did they try to ask? Thoda idea chahiye ki what wording felt less risky.

comments.text: Small practical things helped me — ask for one specific change first, like flexible meeting camera off option or quiet workspace. Put it as productivity tweak, not disability, and copy HR if needed. Keep notes so you can show impact later.

replies.text: Good idea but in my org HR just forwards to managers who then make it awkward. Chalta hai for some teams, others not so much.

comments.text: Masking is exhausting, I feel you. If you can find one manager who seems chill, test with them first, thoda trust build karo before going wider.

postTitle: Frontline teams burning out while HR looks away
postDescription: Last week I watched three shopfloor colleagues hand in resignation emails after another month of double shifts. News says frontline workers are about 70 percent of the workforce but facing high burnout, low engagement and very little HR investment. In my team the training was patchy, pay not competitive and the mobile tools were slow or just plain broken, so people spent more time on admin than actual work. That churn created constant firefighting for managers, more temp hires and worse service on ground. A frontline first approach with fair pay, flexible rostering, real training and mobile friendly HR tech could actually move the needle, but it rarely becomes a priority. Anyone else seen this up close, kya karte ho to stop people from leaving, any low cost fixes that actually worked? 😤

comments.text: That hits home yaar. At my old retail outlet people would quietly stop caring then suddenly quit, no notice. Managers used to ask for headcount but the real issue was roster fairness and no clear travel compensation. Small changes like proper shift swaps and a decent travel allowance helped more than pep talks.

comments.text: Try low friction tech first. Even a simple mobile attendance form and weekly microlearning video reduces confusion. Spot bonuses once a quarter and small recognition rituals work wonders, thoda appreciation goes a long way. Also set clear SLA for manager responses so frontline queries dont get ignored.

replies.text: Agree with offline capable apps. Integrate attendance with payroll otherwise managers end up juggling spreadsheets. Look for platforms with easy onboarding, staff will actually use them.

comments.text: Leadership solution will be a new dashboard and a emotional townhall story. Actual fixes? That would require money and effort, so expect more slides. 😤

replies.text: Do you have a template for that business case? Convincing finance for frontline spends was messy in my org.

comments.text: If hiring is frozen, invest in reskilling. Frontline folks can move to supervisor roles with short focussed training. Also small pay bumps and faster appraisals help in negotiation windows, people notice even thoda increment.

postTitle: When Senior Hiring Still Stops At Referrals
postDescription: Got a DM from a senior recruiter yesterday that made me pause. The gist is simple — senior IT hiring in India is still dominated by private networks and trusted referrals while AI is transforming junior roles. I have seen juniors get AI matched gigs faster, but leadership hiring stays paperless meetings, coffee se introductions and trust ka scene, so outsiders struggle. comments.text: This rings true yaar. In my last company senior roles were mostly friends of friends, while outsider profiles got a polite no read. Managers kept saying cultural fit, which often meant same background and same schools. How do you even start changing that?

postTitle: I quit after hives from extreme burnout
postDescription: My chest tightened during a weekly review and I knew something had to give. Severe burnout in a high pressure estate management role gave me chronic hives for six years, and I finally quit because I am not willing to die for an early retirement. After I left I focused on sleep, real boundaries and slowly shifted into coaching work; the hives faded in about three months, bas yaar health matters more than any title. Has anyone else quit a high stress job for health and then rebuilt their career and savings? How did you manage the fear and conversations with family who wanted security?

comments.text: This story hit me hard, I had panic attacks in office too and took a sabbatical. Took freelance gigs while I figured out next steps, thoda insecure tha but health improved. Emergency fund saved me, seriously start there if you can.

replies.text: Thanks yaar, emergency fund ka scene theek nahi tha for me so I sold some stuff and cut monthly bills, not ideal but it bought time.

comments.text: Practical tiplist: build at least three months runway, pause big subscriptions, talk to creditors if needed, and test coaching with a small client base before quitting full time. Also consider part time consulting while you train, thoda pressure kam rahega.

replies.text: Agree on testing first. Too many people jump ship and then panic, not a flex.

comments.text: Finally choosing your skin over salary, took you long enough 🤦‍♂️. Some people treat burnout like a badge of honor until something breaks.

If you still have any medical records, keep them. In many places documented health issues can help with claims or at least support conversations with future employers about accommodations, kya fayda if you dont keep proof.

replies.text: Good point. I had old docs and dermatologist notes, they helped when I applied for a short term disability payout. Felt awkward but useful.

comments.text: Left for depression two years ago. Worst financial months ever but kids saw a healthier parent, that was worth it. Coaching is slow but scalable, keep at it and network aggressively.
How did you make the jump from estate management to coaching? Any certs or steps you recommend, curious bc I might switch too.

replies.text: I started with free workshops, then a short coach training and lots of unpaid sessions to build testimonials. Slow process, bas credibility bana li to paid clients came.

postTitle: Colleagues at Splash Damage facing major job cuts
postDescription: A friend on the team said the all hands today was painfully quiet and people were just staring at their screens. From what I am hearing, Splash Damage has started a studio wide consultation covering all staff and it is expected to lead to major job losses after earlier layoffs and a cancelled project. Colleagues there are scrambling to update LinkedIn, polishing portfolios, and wondering about notice and severance yaar — lots of panic messages in small groups. A few ex teammates mentioned managers being vague, hiring freezes already in effect, and people quietly exploring freelancing or interviews. Anyone here who has been near a studio consultation, kya tips hai for handling notice periods, negotiating packages, or quickly finding new roles?

comments.text: This sucks yaar. Had similar when PE bought a studio I knew — people with portable skills moved fastest. Update CV, make a one page skill map, reach out to recruiters and old managers, and start short contract gigs if you can. Also set up alerts on job boards and tell a few trusted recruiters you are available.

replies.text: Thanks, that is helpful. Any tips on how to approach recruiters quickly without sounding desperate? Koi specific message template works?
Quick message: one line role youre open to, one line top skills, one line availability. Short and clear works best.

comments.text: Practical steps: map your core skills to roles hiring now, make a tiny portfolio repo, practise 2 common interview questions and one takehome task. Also keep a list of expenses so you know how many weeks you can manage before taking a lower pay contract. Kuch short courses on networking or cloud basics can help if you need to pivot a bit.

replies.text: Agree, and find a couple of Discord or Telegram groups for game gigs. I landed a 3 month contract that way last time.

comments.text: Private equity playbook: acquire, cut, repeat. Yaar, game studios keep getting turned into numbers.

replies.text: Sad but true. Market cycles hit creative teams hard.

comments.text: Consultation has a meaning legally in many places — get written confirmation of timeline, ask HR for the consultation document, check your contract for notice and severance clauses, and document all communication. If UK law applies there are minimum procedures; if they mention redundancies ask for criteria and scoring used. Thoda formal but worth doing now.

replies.text: Friends said HR keeps saying process ongoing and managers are vague. They asked about severance but only got a promise to update later. Should they push for something in writing now?
Yes push. Email follow ups are fine — polite and clear. Keeps record and helps if dispute arises.

comments.text: I had a cancelled project once, ended up doing small freelance work with ex clients and building a tiny pipeline. Took a month to stabilise but portfolio grew. If people can, start talking to studios quietly and do small paid tests to show capability.
Do people think this will slow hiring overall or open more freelance gigs? kya scene hoga in next 6 months?

postTitle: Watching colleagues struggle after Intel layoffs
postDescription: A silence filled the team chat the day people started getting exit mails. From what I am seeing around the industry, several folks were let go at Intel and some of them are dealing with multiple hits at once. People in the team are frantically updating resumes, doing nonstop networking, and applying to hundreds of roles but the response rate is tiny. A few folks I know had the added pressure of family income dropping — one guy lost his job twice and his wife also lost hers the same day, so savings are burning fast, thoda scary. It feels like interview bubbles are forming, salary anchors are slipping, and negotiating power is gone for many. Anyone here gone through this recently or have practical tips for standing out when hundreds apply for the same role?

comments.text: This is brutal, yaar. Saw similar at a buddy's team last year and it drains you mentally and financially. Focus on short contract gigs first, even if pay is lower, to keep cashflow. Also prioritize roles where you can show impact in interviews, not long generic resumes 😔

Two practical things that helped my friend: one, tailor the resume to the JD with 3 bullets showing measurable impact. Two, reach out directly to recruiters on LinkedIn with a 1 line hook and one achievement, not the whole life story. Interviewers see 200 apps, make the first 5 seconds count.

replies.text: Thanks, that 1 line hook idea sounds useful. Koi example line you suggest for a firmware engineer?
Example: Delivered 40 faster boot time across product line saving $1.2M annually — available for senior firmware roles. Short, impact first.

comments.text: Hiring teams: 'We have hundreds of applicants but no time to interview anyone' — classic. Recruitment game is weird, bas sab apply karte rahte hain.

Macro note: big tech layoffs create an interview bottleneck, and companies also freeze lateral hiring briefly which increases competition. Consider short courses for adjacent skills, contract or consulting roles, and target smaller firms where hiring timelines are faster.

replies.text: Agree. Also negotiate for joining bonus or salary review timeline if they lowball now. Many companies are flexible on review at 6 months, try to lock that.

comments.text: My partner faced a similar double hit last year, took months to land something stable. Mental health took a hit, so don't ignore that. Join local meetups, choti networking helps; people refer within circles more than cold apps.
Also check staffing agencies and consultancy gigs, they pay a bit less but get you into steady cashflow and fresh resumes. Keep learning but prioritize paying the bills first.

postTitle: Colleagues at Orbit facing layoffs or pay cuts dilemma
postDescription: An all hands ended with leadership saying hard choices are coming and the room went quiet. From what I am hearing around, Orbit Manufacturing is weighing layoffs versus company wide salary cuts to save costs. Teams are suddenly silent, people are quietly sharing resumes and hoarding institutional knowledge, and some managers are trying to map who is critical. HR is pushing for empathetic communication and balanced cost cutting but morale is already dented, thoda panic bhi hai. This feels like one of those moves that will define culture and hiring for years, candidates will ask twice before joining. Anyone else seen this played out well or badly, kya karna chahiye for teams to survive and keep key people, any practical tips? 😕

comments.text: That silence after an all hands is the worst, yaar. Seen this before at a mid cap firm, and people left in waves after a single round of selective layoffs. If leadership wants trust back they need transparency, like clear timelines and criteria, warna rumors hi chalega.

replies.text: Agree. Even basic FAQs from HR help. No answer is worse than a half answer.

comments.text: Practical playbook I saw work: 1) ask for temporary leadership pay cuts first, 2) offer voluntary separation with decent severance, 3) protect critical roles, 4) freeze hiring only for non critical positions, and 5) push reskilling budget for short term. Also update hiring pitch early so recruiters can manage candidate expectations, otherwise interview bubble bursts.

replies.text: Thanks, this is the kind of list people around me were hoping for. Any tips on how to push leadership to do voluntary exit over forced layoffs, koi template ya approach?
For pushing leadership, get numbers ready. Show short term savings vs long term hiring cost, and model lost productivity from churn. Numbers matter to finance more than sentiment.

comments.text: Oh great, pay cuts. Nothing says trust like asking people to work harder for less. 🤦‍♂️

From an HR angle there are legal and retention points to check, bas thoda careful planning se damage can be limited. Make sure any pay cut policy is documented, uniformly applied, and time bound. Also consider retention bonuses for mission critical folks, even small ones signal intent to keep talent.

replies.text: Retention bonuses work but are expensive. If cash is tight, try deferred bonuses or stock based deferrals, depends on company structure.

comments.text: Empathy talk is fine, but if cuts happen without role plans it kills knowledge. Encourage immediate doc sprints and handover sessions, even pair programming for a week. Hiring markets are hot in some domains, so expect offers to come quickly for good people.

replies.text: Totally. Also make an internal short list of people to cross train, that reduces single point failures.

comments.text: Trust will be broken whichever route they choose, but layoffs feel more permanent. If salary cuts are used do a clear roadmap for restoration tied to revenue targets, otherwise people will just move. For candidates, if hiring continues mention the context in interviews, candidates appreciate honesty.

replies.text: Good point about roadmap and targets. Colleagues were worried about negotiation during interviews, anyone here successfully negotiated better offers knowing company was in cost cut mode?

postTitle: When office parties turn into full blown soap operas
postDescription: Banana bread in the pantry turned into a full on office scandal this week. There was a banana bread bake off that somehow became Bananagate, and other holiday moments spilled into stolen brie, secret Santa misses, and a witnessed indiscretion at the party. I have seen similar scenes at my own team events where the joke quickly becomes awkward and people start avoiding each other, thoda tense for project work. The follow up is worse because small gossip bleeds into who gets picked for client calls and who sits where in meetings. Anyone else have a holiday fail that became office lore and how did you handle it, yaar? 😕

comments.text: This reads like a low budget serial. I once watched coworkers trade secret Santa gifts like smug poker players, yaar. People laugh at the party then avoid sitting next to each other for a week. Office drama levels: soap opera energy. 🤦‍♂️

replies.text: Stapler heist next season. Label everything and prepare for acts of petty revenge.

comments.text: Set clear ground rules before any team event. Label food, keep alcohol optional, ask people not to bring high value gifts and remind everyone this is still a work event. If something crosses a line escalate with facts not gossip, HR cares when it affects work. Small steps can save a lot of awkwardness, bas communicate early.

replies.text: Good tips, I tried a pre event message once and some people laughed but it did cut down the weirdness. Will push a simple set of do and donts next time, thanks yaar.
What if HR is useless or just shrugs it off? Any backup plans?

comments.text: Happened at my old team too. Two seniors crossed a line at a party and it messed up reporting and trust for months. Juniors were stuck in the middle and no one wanted to raise it at first. Felt bad watching good work slow down because everyone kept the conversation at coffee table level.

If the event affects the work environment document dates times who was there and what happened and share that with People or HR. Check the employee handbook for event guidelines and escalation path. If HR does not act escalate to a skip level or use anonymous reporting if available, bas keep records.

replies.text: And what if the manager is the one involved in the incident? Then what do you do without risking your job?

comments.text: Secret Santa equals corporate trust fall and sometimes betrayal. Keep gifts under fifty bucks and drama sols itself, haha.

We made a No Drama potluck rule and assigned one person to be the party point of contact. Sounds extra but it worked, that person handled disputes and weird moments quietly. Saved a lot of follow up awkward chats, yaar.

replies.text: Party cop sounds mildly sadistic but also kind of efficient.

postTitle: Colleagues pushed out after internal exam rules
postDescription: A few folks I know were suddenly told to leave after failing an internal exam. TCS is being accused of using opaque exams with 70 to 80 percent pass thresholds to decide who stays, and FITE wants the company to share papers and scores. From what I am seeing around, teams have gone quiet, hiring talks are more tense, and people are scrambling to upskill or look for other jobs 😕. There are stories of real hardship, families hit financially and sudden exits with no clear proof of marks, and lots of confusion about how the scores were decided, thoda panic ho raha hai yaar. Anyone else seen similar exam based cuts or has advice on how affected folks can push for transparency or protect themselves?

comments.text: If the exams actually decide exits then first step is paper trail. Ask for written scores, mail HR and keep copies. From labour law side there are routes but you need evidence, kya fayda agar sab verbal. Also join collective complaints with FITE, a bunch of small cases together have more weight.

replies.text: People I know did ask HR, got vague replies and no marks shared. Some raised grievances but got generic templates. Anyone here had success forcing release of exam papers or official scorecards?
Keep copies of everything, even chat screenshots. If HR refuses, a lawyer can send a legal notice, that often gets a proper reply fast.

comments.text: This sucks, real people losing income overnight. If someone is affected, try to get emergency support from ex collegues or alumni, PF and last month salary should be checked. Also there are some local legal aid groups who help with labour disputes.

replies.text: Agree. NGOs like some legal clinics help pro bono, and local unions can guide paperwork. Even small legal notice often makes company take it seriously.

comments.text: Practical steps for anyone hit by this: update resume, start applying now, collect all email threads and exam invites, ask HR for scorecard in writing, file a formal grievance. CV ready rakhna, interviews can move fast so dont wait.
Funny that corporate life has school style pass marks now. 70 percent to keep your job, kya scene hai. 🤦‍♂️

replies.text: Right? Next they will give detention slips to seniors. Jokes aside, this is messed up for people with mortgages and kids.

comments.text: From an HR lens thresholds must be validated. If a company uses exams for decisions they should publish test blueprints, sample papers and pass justification. An independent audit of the process would be ideal, otherwise it feels arbitrary and open to bias.

replies.text: Who will pay for audits though, companies rarely volunteer. Maybe regulator push is needed, otherwise its just lip service.

comments.text: This will change hiring conversations. Candidates will ask about job security clauses and assessment criteria. If you are interviewing elsewhere, negotiate notice terms and keep skill proof ready. Also think about short term freelancing until things settle, thoda backup helps.

postTitle: I hired weak interviewers and they became top performers
postDescription: One interview went sideways when the candidate could not answer standard objections and kept fumbling with numbers. I read about a recruiter who did the same thing: hired two candidates who bombed interviews but later became top reps in six months. I have tried hiring for grit before, picked someone who was messy in the interview but came hungry, shadowed seniors and soaked up feedback, thoda extra handholding at start. That person started closing deals by month three and ended up among top sellers, so interviews dont always tell the full story. How do you balance giving second chances with the risk of bad hires in your team, kya approaches worked for you here? 🤷‍♀️

comments.text: Good read. I prefer a short paid trial or a day working with the team before offer, that reveals way more than a 45 minute interview. Also use a simple scorecard so you dont confuse charisma with capability, references matter too, yaar.

replies.text: Exactly. Structured interviews plus a piece of real work reduce noise. Even a half day roleplay or a mock cold call shows process and resilience.
And if you cant do paid trial, give a conditional offer with milestones. Works most of the time, thoda risk but controlled.

comments.text: I hired someone who literally fumbled through the whole interview but had the best attitude, now they mentor juniors. Hiring for hunger is risky but can pay off, bas patience chahiye.

replies.text: Yep this was my experience too. I kept weekly check ins and small measurable goals, helped them build confidence. Not every messy interview is a fail, but you need a plan to support them.

comments.text: Interviews are kabhi kabhi theatre, interviews dont equal outcomes. But hiring based on vibes is lottery, hope you got lucky.

replies.text: Lottery is right if there is no process. Luck helps, but process converts luck into predictable wins. Thoda discipline please.

comments.text: Policy angle: create a rubric that weighs coachability and grit alongside skill. Track time to productivity as a KPI for hires you gave a second chance, so decisions are evidence driven.

Counterpoint: I had two such hires and only one recovered. Not saying dont try, but set a clear probation with outcomes otherwise morale suffers when poor performers linger. Fairness matters to team, yaar.

replies.text: Agree. Second chances should have guardrails, otherwise team trust breaks.

comments.text: Nice call on grit. Sometimes you need to bet on attitude more than smooth answers. Works more than you think 😕

postTitle: Polytechnic grads getting left behind as women surge
postDescription: During an interview panel today I saw three diploma candidates freeze on basic shopfloor scenarios while a girl with a recent upskilling certificate answered confidently. replies.text: Agree. Also try project based hiring — give a simple paid assignment, see who submits and how. It filters motivation quickly and saves time in interviews.

comments.text: If colleges had to include semester long industry projects with signed deliverables, things would change. replies.text: Exactly this. I tried sharing a competency list with a nearby polytechnic and they were open but lacked faculty with practical experience. Maybe short faculty internships in companies could help bridge that gap.

postTitle: Teams are staying put but roles not backfilled
postDescription: During a standup the manager flagged three empty headcount slots and casually said there is no plan to hire. News says involuntary separations drove a lot of churn in 2025 but many employers are not backfilling roles, and voluntary quits actually fell as people started sticking around more. I have seen the fallout first hand — tickets pile up, timelines slip, and everyone does extra work while leadership calls it efficiency. Toxic bosses and bad managers still force people out though, so job hugging is not a real win for productivity or morale. Anyone else seeing this at your company, and how are you coping with the extra load without new hires yaar? 😕

comments.text: Last year my team had the same scene — two people left, no backfills, and suddenly sprint planning felt impossible. We started doing weekly triage, dropping low priority work, and people stayed longer just to keep things afloat. It helped a bit but cost morale, meri team was exhausted. Anyone found a good pitch to get leadership to approve hires without sounding dramatic?

replies.text: We tried the triage route too and it delayed product goals. I ended up presenting missed revenue risk numbers and still had to fight, kya scene. If you have a template for that pitch plis share.

comments.text: We stopped hiring but invested in cross training and a bench of contractors for spikes. Also started gating new feature requests — product and sales had to justify impact in writing before we took it on. It is not perfect but reduced burnout. Try documenting time lost to context switching and show cost of delay, that helped me in negotiations.

replies.text: This. Contractors for spikes saved us last quarter. Also run a simple cost per ticket calc and share with finance.

comments.text: Nice logic: remove roles, expect same output. Kya fayda of efficiency if nobody can breathe. 😂

From HR side these freezes often mask cost cutting after involuntary exits. Recommend tracking voluntary quit drivers separately from involuntary numbers, and run pulse surveys to catch toxicity early. Also align hiring ask to OKRs and show the opportunity cost of delayed projects to make a stronger case.

replies.text: What pulse questions worked for you? We tried but got generic answers.
Ask about workload, support from manager, growth opportunities. Keep it short and anonymous, then act fast on the red flags.

comments.text: I stayed because I needed the stability but ended up burned out and applied elsewhere quietly. Managers praised commitment publicly but never fixed the issues. Lesson learnt: your CV matters more than loyalty when leadership is toxic, bas yaar take care of yourself.

replies.text: That hit close. Same here, stayed to help the team but it cost me a year of mental energy. How did you handle exit conversations? I worry about burning bridges.
I kept feedback factual in exit, gave handover docs, and stayed professional. It worked, no drama.

comments.text: If productivity drops because people hug jobs, measure outcome not hours. Use cycle time, throughput, customer tickets closed as metrics. When you show a 20 percent drop in output per person managers listen. Also skilling can help but only if managers support time for learning.

postTitle: Candidate Said Water in an Interview Today
postDescription: Facepalm moment in an interview today. Interviewer asked the usual icebreaker about favourite drink and when the candidate answered Water the interviewer dismissed it, told them to try harder and basically ended the call. I was on the hiring panel and watching that exchange made me rethink how many small biases we let slide in live interviews and how performative answers are favoured over honest ones, thoda ajeeb laga. Anyone else seen this, and how do you handle these moments so you are fair but not awkward? 😕

comments.text: Happened to me last month, candidate said water and the panel literally acted like they had failed an unseen test. People expect quirky answers now, kya fayda of honesty if that gets penalised. Treating small talk like a personality exam is getting out of hand.

replies.text: Yeah that was my thought too. I tried to steer it back to role based questions but the interviewer seemed judgemental. Felt awkward to intervene without sounding like I was defending the candidate.
If you are on panel push for rubric scores not vibes. Short term fix is to ask a concrete follow up like Why that drink, what does it say about working style. Makes it less performative.

comments.text: Guess the interviewer wanted 'chai latte with almond milk and a side hustle' answer. 😂

Practical thing I do as an interviewer is set a scoring sheet for every round and make everyone fill it before discussing. That reduces these spontaneous opinion kills. Also add a note that small talk is optional so honest answers dont get penalised.

replies.text: Totally. We use a 1 to 5 for clarity, problem solving, culture fit and communication. If someone bombs the icebreaker but nails the technicals the score shows it.

comments.text: Empathy angle here — candidates are nervous, cultural differences exist. Water could be an honest answer or even a way to avoid alcohol mention. Interviewer should not make it a character test. Thoda human bano yaar.
Maybe the candidate was trolling or testing reaction. But even then, calling them out and ending the call is unprofessional. Better to note it and move on or ask a role related question.

replies.text: Agree. If someone is being weird, ask for clarification rather than shutting down. You might uncover anxiety or communication issues but with dignity.

comments.text: This screams need for interviewer training. Clear behavioral anchors, bias awareness, and mock panels. Even a 30 minute calibration every week helps reduce these 'gut reaction' endings.

postTitle: Colleagues rattled after IndiGo operational meltdown
